name: Micro-dosed growth hormone

card.summary: Using small amounts of prescription human growth hormone, usually for anti-aging, leaner body composition and recovery, with a firmer, younger and less fatty look as the stated goal.
card.note: Growth hormone is a prescription drug; non-prescribed use is outside approved indications and gray-market products carry additional risks.

quick.overview:
Micro-dosed growth hormone (low-dose HGH) is the use of small quantities of recombinant human growth hormone, a prescription peptide, as an anti-aging or body-composition strategy. Proponents aim for leaner midsections, fuller-looking muscle, better skin and joint recovery, expecting to avoid the side effects associated with larger replacement or bodybuilding amounts.

Research on low-dose GH exists mainly in patient groups. A pilot study in men with HIV-associated lipodystrophy used a low daily dose and reported improved fat distribution and higher IGF-I; trials in healthy people seeking appearance benefit are lacking. On looksmax forums, some users also ask about low-dose GH for height in teenagers, a use that approved treatment covers only for specific growth conditions.
quick.how: In patient settings, GH is a prescribed injectable given under endocrinology supervision, with IGF-I blood levels used to guide adjustment. Online communities describe self-directed use paired with training, and some pair it with growth-hormone-releasing peptides such as CJC-1295. This article does not cover amounts, schedules or sourcing.
quick.risks: Growth hormone can reduce insulin sensitivity and cause fluid retention and joint pain, effects reported in lipodystrophy and other studies that used higher doses. The FDA has approved GH only for specific conditions, and medical reviews note that safety and effectiveness in healthy adults are not established. Products sold outside prescription channels may be mislabelled or counterfeit.

lead: Micro-dosed growth hormone, also called low-dose HGH, refers to taking small amounts of recombinant human growth hormone as an anti-aging or body-composition protocol rather than as treatment for a diagnosed deficiency. People who practice it say they are after a leaner look, firmer skin, better recovery and more muscle, while staying under the amounts that produce the joint pain and glucose problems reported at standard replacement levels [1].

Growth hormone therapy is approved for conditions such as childhood growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure, Prader-Willi syndrome, idiopathic short stature and AIDS-related wasting in adults [2]. Replacement in deficient adults can increase muscle mass and reduce fat tissue, but a long-term mortality benefit has not been shown [2]. Anti-aging promotion began after a 1990 trial in older men and a 1997 book, and a 2003 pair of New England Journal of Medicine editorials stated that evidence of safety and efficacy in healthy adults was lacking [2].

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it from two angles: low-dose GH combined with androgens and peptides to improve facial and body masculinity, and low-dose GH to add height in adolescence [3][4]. Bodybuilding forums such as T Nation discuss it for recovery and body composition [13]. Published research on low-dose GH comes from clinical populations, not from people seeking cosmetic changes.

angle.text: Users say low-dose GH helps them look leaner and more recovered by improving the ratio of fat to muscle and skin quality. Patient studies show body-composition changes, but cosmetic use in healthy people has not been tested.

paras: Micro-dosing here means using amounts below the usual therapeutic range, with the aim of raising growth hormone and IGF-I toward the upper normal range instead of well above it. In the 2004 pilot study, six men with HIV-associated lipodystrophy received a daily low dose of subcutaneous hGH for 16 weeks, and total IGF-I rose about twofold to the top of the normal range [1].

There is no standard definition of micro-dosing; the term is used by forum members and by anti-aging marketers for regimens they regard as smaller than medical replacement. This article does not cover specific amounts, schedules or sourcing.

sections.h: History of growth hormone and its off-label use
paras: Before the 1980s, GH came from human pituitary glands. From 1963 to 1985 about 7,700 children in the US and some 27,000 worldwide received this cadaver-derived hormone, until four young US adults who had received it developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in 1985 and its use stopped [2]. Genentech's recombinant product Protropin was approved the same year, at a cost of US$10,000 to $30,000 a year, followed by products from Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Novo and Serono [2].

Anti-aging interest followed a 1990 study by Rudman of men over 60 that drew wide attention [2]. In 1997 Ronald Klatz of the American Academy of Anti-Aging Medicine published Grow Young With HGH, which Wikipedia describes as an uncritical endorsement, and the internet then amplified the claims [2]. In 2003 two New England Journal of Medicine editorials criticised advertisements for HGH-releasing supplements and noted the lack of evidence that HGH is safe and effective in healthy or elderly adults [2]. In August 2011 the FDA said evidence on increased risk of death was inconclusive [2].

In sport, Dan Duchaine's 1982 Underground Steroid Handbook is cited as the first description of GH as a doping agent, and the International Olympic Committee banned it in 1989; because recombinant GH matches the body's own sequence, it is harder to detect than anabolic steroids [12].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: One looksmax.org thread proposes combining low-dose GH or CJC-1295 with androgens and low-dose testosterone to masculinize the face over time as an alternative to surgery [3]. Another asks about low-dose GH at age 13 for height, citing a study in children with growth disorders; replies note cost and the difficulty of obtaining it as a minor [4]. These are users' claims; GH use for height has been studied in conditions such as idiopathic short stature, and registered trials of low-dose and long-acting GH have enrolled children with growth deficits [5][6].

On T Nation, one long thread on GH has posters crediting it with better recovery from training, and one reply to a poster of about forty says it leans toward trying it for six months while noting that much of the literature relating GH and IGF-1 to outcomes is epidemiological [13]. A separate T Nation thread asks whether GH can cause facial changes at low or normal doses, and a poster there reports that secretagogues did not move his levels and that for him it was GH or nothing [14].

Looksmaxxing posts often place GH in a stack with testosterone, DHT-derived androgens and peptides, with the stated aim of a more dimorphic face or a leaner body; the thread cited above also notes the need for hair, acne and collagen protection with such a stack [3].

In the 2004 pilot study of HIV lipodystrophy, patients on low-dose hGH reported improved lipodystrophy, with a lower waist-to-thigh ratio, a higher ratio of peripheral to trunk soft tissue and higher HDL cholesterol [1].

In adults with GH deficiency, replacement increases muscle mass and bone density and reduces adipose tissue, and a large study found no overall rise in cancer risk over short follow-up though some subgroups had higher risk [2]. In people without deficiency, Wikipedia's summary of the sports literature says studies show less body fat and more lean mass but no gain in muscle strength, that part of the lean-mass gain may reflect fluid retention, and that a 2008 meta-analysis by Liu and colleagues concluded claims of improved physical performance were not supported [12].

For height, Eli Lilly-sponsored trials in the late 1990s in children with extreme idiopathic short stature reported adult-height gains of 4 to 8 cm after roughly four years of treatment, and the FDA approved Humatrope for idiopathic short stature in 2003, an indication that remains controversial [2]. A 1983 report described low-dose HGH in children with somatotropin deficiency [15], and registered trials include GH in children born small for gestational age and in Turner syndrome [16][17].

GH usually reduces insulin sensitivity; a 1999 critical-care study reported higher mortality in treated ICU patients, and a large study found elevated cancer risk in some subgroups such as under 35 or childhood-onset deficiency [2]. High-dose hGH in the lipodystrophy literature was linked to joint pain and glucose intolerance, which the low-dose approach was designed to limit [1]. Long-term misuse in sport can mimic acromegaly, with swelling of the hands and feet, joint pain, fluid retention and sweating, though the same source notes that side effects of medical therapy may be overstated because earlier studies used very high doses [12]. A dog study found chronic low-dose infusion of recombinant 22K hGH raised fasting glucose transiently and produced marked insulin resistance [8].

GH is a prescription drug approved only for specific conditions [2]. Products sold outside prescription channels may be counterfeit; Wikipedia says fraudulent versions may have been sold in gyms and that the internet spawned many anti-aging frauds [2].

In the 2004 pilot study of HIV lipodystrophy, patients on low-dose hGH reported improved lipodystrophy, with a lower waist-to-thigh ratio, a higher ratio of peripheral to trunk soft tissue and higher HDL cholesterol [1].

A 1977 study in five osteoporosis patients found no significant gain in total body calcium on a low-dose GH regimen but gains on a high-dose one [7]. A dog study reported that chronic low-dose infusion of recombinant 22K hGH raised fasting glucose transiently and produced marked insulin resistance [8].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists low-dose GH trials in adult GH deficiency (a phase 3 comparison of low and conventional dosing in 112 patients) and in obese PCOS and metabolic syndrome (both withdrawn) [9][10][11]. No trial has examined micro-dosed GH in healthy adults for appearance.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, low-dose GH is discussed as a way to get benefits for recovery, leanness, height and facial structure with fewer side effects than full replacement [3][4][13].

claims.claim: Small amounts give a leaner, firmer, more recovered look
claims.believers: T Nation posters credit GH with better recovery, and one suggests a six-month trial [13].
claims.experts: Adults with deficiency gain muscle and lose fat on replacement, and sports-literature summaries report less body fat and more lean mass without added strength, partly from fluid [2][12].

claims.claim: Low doses avoid the side effects of full-dose GH
claims.believers: Proponents cite the lipodystrophy pilot as showing benefit at the top of the normal IGF-I range [1].
claims.experts: The pilot used six patients; GH usually lowers insulin sensitivity and a dog study found low-dose infusion produced insulin resistance [1][2][8].

claims.claim: Low-dose GH adds height in teenagers
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster cites a children's study for gains of up to 8 cm [4].
claims.experts: Trials in extreme idiopathic short stature reported 4 to 8 cm adult-height gains over roughly four years in children with growth disorders; none has tested healthy adolescents [2].

claims.claim: GH plus DHT-derived androgens masculinises the face over time
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread proposes the stack as an alternative to jaw surgery for androgynous faces [3].
claims.experts: No published study has tested this combination for facial structure.

claims.claim: GH at low or normal doses can change facial features
claims.believers: A T Nation thread asks the question and one poster says only HGH moved his levels [14].
claims.experts: Long-term misuse in sport is reported to mimic acromegaly with swelling of hands and feet; no study has examined low doses for facial change [12].

claims.claim: GH is an anti-aging treatment for healthy adults
claims.believers: Anti-aging clinics and Klatz's 1997 book promoted it for rejuvenation [2].
claims.experts: Two 2003 NEJM editorials said evidence of safety and efficacy in healthy or elderly adults was lacking, and the FDA called mortality evidence inconclusive in 2011 [2].
